fields.Thread: Three books built out of other books that say so, and that disagree about what the store of already-said language does to the person copying it. For Burton the compiled cento is medicine ('I write of melancholy, by being busy to avoid melancholy'); for Flaubert encyclopedic copying is the disease, ending in two clerks at the desk and a Dictionary of Accepted Ideas; for Mullen the dictionary and the thesaurus are partners in bed, and Flaubert's stock phrase comes back emptied in 'Elliptical'.
fields.Themes: cento, copying, commonplace, dictionary, encyclopedia, cliché, melancholy of scholars, alphabetical order, compilation, received ideas

3. Heinsius's 'very lap of eternity' vs. the clerks who 'wanted to know the exact number of volumes': describe a third posture toward a library as a single gesture.

fields.Thread: How do two things that never touch stay in step? Geulincx's two clocks chime together 'without any causality' because one artificer built both. Bell (via Casimir's egg and alarm clock, 'I, the great chef, imposed a structure on my kitchen') meets the same structure as option (3), superdeterminism, and refuses it. Harman names the tradition, occasionalism, and makes Latour its 'first secular occasionalist': the gaps are real and local mediators close them, fallibly. One artificer, no artificer, many small artificers.
fields.Themes: occasionalism, two clocks, correlation vs causation, superdeterminism, free will, pre-established harmony, vicarious causation, mediation, Beckett, gesture and will
fields.Notebook_Prompts:
1. The will's clock: using Geulincx's 'I do not know how such a thing is brought about...' (p. 33), write a gesture of your own (a hand lifting a pen) three ways: occasionalist, Bell's option 3, Latourian. What does the gesture mean in each?
2. Superdeterminism as an ethics: Bell treats option (3) as a reductio ('our apparent free will is entangled with them'); Geulincx builds a morality from the same premise (ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis). Write the ethics Bell refused; which Beckett sentence is its motto?
3. The chef: Casimir's 'great chef' arranges the coincidence; Harman says a Latourian bridge can fail ('an interesting tragic side of causation that was always denied ... to God'). Write a short fiction of a failed synchronization.

fields.Thread: What is left when the apparatus that certifies a work and the work it certifies come apart. Zweig's blind collector points 'to the millimetre' to the collectors' stamps (Nagler, Remy, Esdaile) on the back of a blank sheet: provenance without the object. Perec's forger has certificates for everything ('They had them') but cannot make 'an authentic masterwork of the past': the object without its provenance, and the one mark he cannot copy is Antonello's 'me pinxit'. Krauss names the machinery ('to find the mark, the warrant, the certification of the original') and argues the original was always propped on the copy (Rodin casts, the vintage print, the grid; 'spontaneity was the most fakable of signifieds'). Conflict: Krauss dissolves the original; the councillor and Winckler each stake a life on it, and in both fictions the belief produces something real. Zweig's portfolios are prints, already multiples: the medium in which Krauss, quoting Benjamin, says asking for the authentic print 'makes no sense'.
fields.Themes: authenticity, originality, copy, forgery, provenance, collectors' marks, certification, prints and multiples, aura, Benjamin, spontaneity, gesture, catalogue

2. A recipe for your spontaneity: Winckler fails at 'that celebrated tautness in the jaw' and gets 'my own face'; Krauss: 'spontaneity was the most fakable of signifieds' (p. 167). Write one of your unforgeable gestures as instructions for a forger, then what the instructions leave out.
3. The catalogue as tombstone: 'Just promise me to draw up a handsome catalogue: it will be my tombstone'. Draft five entries of the councillor's catalogue raisonné for sheets that no longer exist; set one beside Borges's list of Pierre Menard's visible works.

fields.Thread: A personification is a machine that turns many particulars into one speaking body. Breen describes the machine (medieval personifications as tools of thought, sorted by the universals debate into Platonic, Aristotelian/nominalist and 'Prudentian' types; 'We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us'). Erasmus's Folly is the machine taking the floor: an abstraction that refuses definition ('a sketch which would be a mere shadow of myself when I am here before you'), mocks the 'realists, nominalists, Thomists…' whose quarrel Breen uses to classify her, and ends 'forgetting who I am'. Michaux's Plume runs it backwards: a particular 'not imposing enough or universal enough to assume outright allegorical significance' (Sieburth), whose name slides into initials (A., once 'Eache'; G.; B.), and whose author concludes 'SELF is but a point of equilibrium … An averaged "self," a crowd movement.' Traffic runs downward in Breen, sideways in Erasmus, upward in Michaux. Conflict: 'I am myself wherever I am' vs 'There is no self.'
fields.Themes: personification, prosopopoeia, universals, nominalism, allegory as machine, persona, heteronym, self as crowd, folly, names and initials, mock encomium, Prudentius

fields.Thread: Three books on how continuous language gets cut, at three scales. Parkes: the pause, punctuation as signs for a reader who has lost the speaker ('Its primary function is to resolve structural uncertainties in a text'). Szendy: the point (stigmē, from stizein, to prick, bruise) as the blow that makes experience ('It is force; it is power; it is political decision'). Dames: the chapter as a technology of time ('Our comprehension of time is continually and inescapably punctuated and divided'). Genealogy: Szendy and Dames both cite Parkes, and ¶ is C for capitulum, so the chapter's mark shrank into the paragraph sign while the chapter grew. Shared case: Tristram Shandy (Parkes's elocutionary dashes; Szendy's sash-window cut, 'the button point is unbuttoned'; Dames's chapter upon chapters on the stairs, 'a continuing motion or gesture caught midway'). Conflict: for Parkes the mark serves comprehension, for Szendy it constitutes the subject, and Dames puts the break in lived time.
fields.Themes: punctuation, pause, point, stigma, chapter, segmentation, capitulum, pilcrow, Tristram Shandy, Sterne, gesture, time, reading, Lacan point de capiton, scriptio continua
fields.Notebook_Prompts:

2. The landing: short chapters, each under five hundred words like Sterne's chapter upon chapters, each breaking midgesture (Dames pp. 161–63). Does the break register the gesture ('the doubling blow', Szendy p. 4) or make it?
3. The fossil in the pilcrow: ¶ is C for capitulum (Parkes p. 305) while the chapter swelled (Dames Table 3.1). Write on a sign that forgot what it stood for, or on Augustine's finger calling up a capitulum where the page marked nothing (Dames p. 63).

fields.Thread: Three answers to Hooke's Micrographia (1665), which is not in the library and sits in the middle as a gap; each refuses the lens differently. Cavendish (Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, 1666): the glass deludes; 'a natural Eye' and 'regular Reason' will do, and 'no Microscope is able to give us a true information' of inward actions. Swift (1726): abolish the instrument by resizing the observer; in Brobdingnag Gulliver sees lice 'with my naked Eye, much better than those of an European Louse through a Microscope', gets nausea rather than knowledge, and becomes the lens himself ('whose large Opticks were not so acute as mine'). Leskov ('The Steel Flea', 1881): the craftsman surpasses the instrument ('we just sharpened our eyes'); Lefty's nails are 'too small for any nitroscope', so the finest work is invisible and unsigned, and it stops the flea dancing. Conflict: deceives / disgusts / surpassed. Structural: in each book the unaided eye wins and pays for it.
fields.Themes: microscope, telescope, naked eye, magnification, scale, flea, louse, Hooke, Micrographia, Royal Society, experimental philosophy, craft, the hand, skaz, malapropism, proportion of distance, Benjamin's Storyteller

3. The shod flea won't dance: 'calculated for the most accurate exactness, and it can't carry the flea-shoes' (§15); Cavendish, 'Man ... spoils Nature with doting too much upon Art' (p. 4). Improve a finished text until it stops moving, then write the workmen's note on the cost.

fields.Thread: Three books made of beginnings and nothing else. Calvino's Flannery states the wish ('I would like to be able to write a book that is only an incipit', ch. 8) and If on a winter's night a traveler half-grants it with ten broken-off first chapters. Kuppner's Arioflotga carries it out for verse: 4,108 first lines of a lost 'Great Anthology', alphabetized, with no poems behind them (the title is the initials of 'A Revised Index Of First Lines Of The Great Anthology'). Jullien's The Book of Beginnings does it for philosophy, a whole book on three first sentences (Genesis, Hesiod's Theogony, the Yijing), built on the claim 'We never exit a first sentence.' Conflict: for Calvino the incipit's charge is narrative, 'the promise of a time of reading'; Jullien's Chinese opening 'opens no account', because 'No negative means no "story."' Kuppner sits between: promises with nothing promised, alphabet in place of plot, and two stock first lines ('O Muse, begin'; 'At first, in the beginning, there was no such thing as Time') that parody Jullien's two Western openings.
fields.Themes: incipit, first lines, first sentence, beginnings, index, alphabetical order, narrative promise, Genesis, Hesiod, Yijing, creation vs generation vs process, copyist, commonplace, Oblivia, second person
fields.Notebook_Prompts:

3. The copyist's hand: Flannery copies the start of Crime and Punishment to see 'if the charge of energy contained in that start is communicated to my hand' (ch. 8). fields.Thread: Three texts about a gesture that is lost and the attempts to get it back. Kleist (1810): consciousness spoils grace; the youth at the mirror cannot repeat his own pose; grace returns only in the marionette (no consciousness) or the god (infinite consciousness), 'once perception, as it were, has traversed the infinite'. Agamben (1992): 'By the end of the nineteenth century, the Western bourgeoisie had definitely lost its gestures'; cinema 'tries at once to reclaim what it has lost and to record its loss'; gesture is neither facere nor agere but gerere, 'the exhibition of a mediality', at bottom a gag. McCarthy, Remainder (2005): a man who must relearn every movement ('No Doing without Understanding') envies De Niro's seamless gestures and hires re-enactors to stage scenes until he feels 'real'; the liver lady drops her bag on the third repetition, as Kleist's youth fails on his. Conflict: return via the infinite (Kleist), via cinema and pure means (Agamben), via endless rehearsal (McCarthy), which yields 'votive' gestures that never arrive. Agamben never cites Kleist in Means Without End; the bridge is built here.
fields.Themes: gesture, grace, marionette, consciousness, repetition, re-enactment, cinema, Tourette, Muybridge, Warburg, facere/agere/gerere, mediality, gag, authenticity, second-hand, weightlessness, Spinario

fields.Thread: Three stories in which a man from the city or from Europe takes a wound to the head and then goes into the Argentine plain, which he already knows as a picture. Borges, 'The South' (1953): Dahlmann's forehead is brushed in the dark ('a bat? a bird?'), septicemia follows, and he takes the train to a South he knows through 'nostalgic, literary knowledge'; an old gaucho throws him a dagger. Aira, An Episode in the Life of a Landscape Painter (2000): Rugendas, Humboldt's physiognomic painter, is struck twice by lightning, survives on morphine with a ruined face, draws an Indian raid under a lace mantilla, and near the end 'A bat coming in the opposite direction brushed gently against his forehead', which answers Borges's question. Bolaño, 'The Insufferable Gaucho' (2003): an ex-judge leaves Buenos Aires in the 2001 collapse, weeps over the store in 'The South', finds 'no horses left here … only rabbits', and stabs a writer back in the city. Genealogy: Bolaño's named rewrite; Bolaño's preface opens the Aira volume; Chris Andrews translated both. Shared form: wound, then a plain already pictured, then a face-to-face ending.

fields.Thread: Three books on what a mind does when an animal arrives before its category, or a category arrives without its animal. Physiologus (Greek, perhaps 2nd c. AD; trans. Curley 1979): the unicorn as a 'nature' with no body, 'a small animal like the kid', caught in a virgin's lap, one-horned 'because the Savior said, "I and the Father are one"'; Curley's note: 'The legend of the unicorn arises out of reports concerning the rhinoceros.' Eco, Kant and the Platypus (1997): Polo meets that rhinoceros on Java, calls it a unicorn, and denies the virgin's-lap legend ('He has modified the intension and left the extension unchanged', p. 58); then the platypus's eighty-odd years of negotiation, 1797–1884. Gombrich, 'Truth and the Stereotype' (Art and Illusion, 1960): Dürer's rhinoceros, armoured from 'the dragon with its armoured body', copied into natural histories until the 18th century; copying 'proceeds through the rhythms of schema and correction'. Agreement: Gombrich and Eco both start from Kant's schematism (Gombrich's epigraph; Eco ch. 2), and Eco cites 'the classic example in Gombrich' (p. 348). Genealogy: the Physiologus is the book Polo carried to Java. They disagree about what a type is for: meaning (Physiologus), making (Gombrich), negotiation (Eco).

fields.Thread: Three books about a severed head shown to a crowd, and three answers to what the crowd should do with it. Kadare, The Traitor's Niche (1978): the Ottoman state displays rebels' heads in a niche by an obelisk in the capital; the courier Tundj Hata rents Ali Pasha's head to frontier villages, for whom 'this spectacle was at the same time their literature, theater, art, philosophy, and perhaps love' (ch. 3). Lu Xun, Jottings under Lamplight: the Sendai slide of a man 'about to be decapitated by a Japanese soldier' (p. 20) and strong, apathetic onlookers turns him from medicine to literature; later, 'the only cure is to give them nothing to watch' (p. 261). The Sacred Conspiracy (Bataille/Acéphale, 1936–39): an annual festival proposed for the guillotining of Louis XVI, the king's 'supposed skull' to be left at the Concorde obelisk (p. 113), and 'Man has escaped his head like a condemned man escaping from prison' (p. 125). Conflict: the empire sells the spectacle, Lu Xun refuses it, Bataille restages it as rite. Structural: each is unsure of its head (Ali's buried by a dervish; Hurshid's exhumed after forty hours; Lu Xun's slide never found and elsewhere described as a shooting, Editors' Intro p. 8; Acéphale's skull only 'supposed'). No book cites another; the bridge is built here.

fields.Thread: Three books in which a made thing exists because it is described, and in which grammar decides whose hands made it. Roby, Technical Ekphrasis (2016): Greek and Roman machine prose; Philo makes the reader see his artillery 'even if he never builds the machine' (p. 214); passives and third-person imperatives create 'a depopulated or impersonal construction space, in which the artifact seems to come together without human intervention' (p. 205); the Helping Hand, 'not about what we can do, but about what can be done'; Hero's automata 'designed to mystify an audience' (p. 5). Roussel, Impressions of Africa (1910): technical ekphrasis of machines that exist only in prose and were generated by puns ('language itself is the sole motor and guide', Polizzotti); Bedu's river loom, 'Invisibly moved by the driving belts' (ch. VI), weaves the Flood/shipwreck and runs 'without aid or supervision' (ch. X); Louise's lensless painting machine (ch. IX); the novel is built like an automaton theatre, with the performance (I–IX) before the mechanism (X–XXVI). Levé, Works (2002): 533 works 'conceived but not brought into being' (#1), 271 of 517 parsed entries opening in the agentless passive; #418 weaves a tapestry of a homonym of Roussel, a double of doubles. Shared method (description as fabrication), genealogy (Roussel to Levé), structural (the passive voice as an ethics of agency). They disagree about what a description owes the world: buildable (Roby's authors), 'nothing real' (Roussel), building left to whoever wants it (Levé).

fields.Thread: Three books on 1930s Southern tenancy and the printed wish-images that passed into the tenant house, and the printed book that later passed back. Agee, Cotton Tenants (written 1936 for Fortune, killed, pub. 2013): opens on Lucile Burroughs's third-grade geography reader, Around the World With the Children; on the Burroughs wall a Peters Shoes calendar girl, 'Title: Cherie. Subtitle (written twice, in pencil): Lucile.' (ch. 2). Crews, A Childhood (1978): a boy born 1935 in Bacon County, Georgia, and Willalee Bookatee (son of the Black tenant family on the Crews place) turn the Sears 'Wish Book' into a saga of feuds, because 'all the people in its pages were perfect' and 'under those fancy clothes there had to be scars' (ch. Four). Maharidge & Williamson, And Their Children After Them (1989): the book returns to its subjects; Junior 'fumed that it made them look like slaves'; Fred Ricketts, nearly blind, 'kept looking at Evans's pictures'; Maggie Louise (Agee's Lucile) read her mother's copy before her death in 1971; a section opens on a 1941 USDA reader, 'Round the World with Cotton, found in an abandoned school. Three positions on one motif: visitor (Agee) inventories the pictures, child inside (Crews) rewrites them, return (Maharidge) records the subjects reading their own picture. Crews's children do to the catalogue what documentary does to its subjects, in reverse: they add the scars. Agee to Maharidge is genealogy; the Crews bridge is built here (neither text mentions the other).

fields.Thread: Three books on one archive, and on where in it the two anthropologists stand. Cook's own journal (Penguin selection, ed. Edwards, from Beaglehole) ends 17 Jan 1779 mid-scene: 'Touahah took me by the hand and conducted me to a large Morai, the other gentlemen with Parea and four or five more of the Natives followed.' Lono/Orono/Erono occurs 0 times in his journal text in this edition, and 11 times in Edwards's Postscript, which has to reconstruct the Hikiau rite, the return and the death from King, Samwell, Burney et al. Sahlins, Islands of History (1985), fills the silence with structure: 'Cook indeed became the image of Lono' (p. 105), and his death has 'the properties of a ritual transformation' (p. 106). Obeyesekere, Cannibal Talk (2005), extending Apotheosis (1992): the Lono myth 'was not constructed in Hawai‘i but in London' (p. 18); his test case is a scene Cook did write, the quarterdeck at Queen Charlotte Sound, 23 Nov 1773, where Cook had flesh broiled 'being desireous of being an eye wittness to a fact which many people had their doubts about.' Sahlins settles where Cook stops writing, Obeyesekere where Cook stages proof. Both name the conflict: Sahlins's ch. 4 epigraph (Home's log), the accounts 'so Exceedingly perplexed ... that it was a hard matter to Colect Certainty' (p. 104); Obeyesekere, 'what I read adds to my confusion as surely as it adds to Sahlins’s clarity' (p. 168). Neither book is the famous exchange itself (1992/1995); one comes before it, one after, with the journal as shared ground. Edwards's Postscript gives a third, practical answer: 'He brought them iron, and they used it to kill him.'

fields.Thread: One symptom, two diagnoses. Kafka's diary entry for 7 June 1912 ('7 June. Bad. Wrote nothing today. Tomorrow no time.') is the epigraph to Flaherty's chapter on writer's block (The Midnight Disease, ch. 3), where block means not writing while able to AND suffering for it. Vila-Matas's narrator in Bartleby & Co. (note 24) quotes another empty diary day, the rainy Sunday of 7 Jan 1912 ('staring at my fingers', Goethe), as proof that Kafka had 'Bartleby's syndrome': not-writing as a vocation of the demanding conscience, a 'disease' with the suffering clause left out. Both later books are first-person diaries or case histories of a writing disorder, and both quote Kafka through a channel that shows: Flaherty's Kafka is a composite (Diaries; Felice letters via Leader; a line that matches Janouch more closely than the Diaries), and Vila-Matas's reaches English via Spanish. Machine counts of the Diaries show writing discussed most in 1911–12 (44/86, 32/73 entries) and almost never in 1922, the year of The Castle (5/73).

fields.Thread: Three boxes of cards. Krajewski (Paper Machines) explains why the slip box, unlike the book, is a machine and a 'second memory' that surprises its own author ('index cards know more than their author'). Nabokov's 118 Oxford dream cards (Oct 14 1964 – Jan 3 1965, Dunne experiment) and Barthes's quartered-paper Mourning Diary (from Oct 26 1977) are two such boxes, used as instruments for catching time when it misbehaves: one an experiment hunting time's backflow, the other a vigil subjected to it. Nabokov's 1968 note on a 1964 card ('Had quite forgotten this when inventing Ardis') and Barthes's 'mourning in layers... Units' / 'discontinuous character' are that surprise in practice. Both stacks silt up (machine counts: Nabokov's numbered records flatten after mid-Nov; Barthes's dated headings fall from 72 in the first five weeks to near zero after the anniversary). Both were ordered posthumously by editors (Léger corrected the order). Krajewski names Nabokov once, as the 'apotheosis' of the novelist's card box; he never reaches the dream cards, and Barthes isn't in his book.

fields.Thread: Three books whose only archive is other people's mouths. Kapuściński (Travels with Herodotus) takes Herodotus as the first reporter and catalogues his hedges ('If this is true, I don't know. I write only that which is said', ch. 18). Portelli (They Say in Harlan County; title from Florence Reece's 'They say in Harlan County') sets the oral historian's rules: 'never putting into people's mouths words they did not actually say', and 'What people believe and what they forget is as significant as what people recall accurately.' Mitchell (Up in the Old Hotel) gives the negative case: Joe Gould's 'Oral History' of 'things I heard people say' that Mitchell concludes 'doesn't exist' (Lepore 2016 disputes this), plus Mitchell's own composite Mr. Flood, 'truthful rather than factual', and his own unwritten novel. fields.Thread: Who is allowed to hear the siren? Blanchot's Ulysses hears the Sirens' 'song only still to come' safely, tied to the mast, while the oarsmen have 'only a right to the pleasure of watching their leader writhe ridiculously' (Book to Come pp. 3–9). Rancière's Mallarmé makes the 'discrete siren' the emblem of a poem waiting for 'a crowd still to come' and refuses the Saint-Simonian hymn of 'Industry made religious; religion made industrial' (pp. 5, 28, 33–34). Avraamov's Baku Symphony of Sirens (7 Nov 1922) carried that hymn out with a whole city's whistles, foghorns, artillery and choirs, conducted from a tower with flags; he 'did not want spectators' (booklet PDF p. 22), yet in Moscow 1923 the melodies were 'completely unrecognizable to the masses'. Shared figure (siren as lure, poem, factory whistle) + conflict over the one and the many (mast, conductor, tower) + genealogy (Blanchot's Mallarmé → Rancière; Saint-Simon → Proletkult). Twist: Avraamov's main instrument was tuned steam whistles ('Sinfonia Gudki'); 'sirens do not exist, except in the writings of poets.'

fields.Thread: Three attempts to make a work of nothing, each of which ends up describing a reader who fills it in. Lem's A Perfect Vacuum (1971) reviews Solange Marriot's nonexistent Rien du tout, a novel of pure negation: 'a critique of a book that not only does not exist but also cannot.' Dworkin's No Medium (2013) reads real blank books, erasures and silent records, and closes with 'Further Listening,' a discography of silences written in record-review voice. Cloninger's Some Ways of Making Nothing (2021) sorts 'flavors of qualitative nothing' and calls making nothing a braking of becoming, as opposed to abstaining. Exact links: the blank turns erotic in the reader (Marriot's railway station / Cocteau's Nudisme); and a three-way quarrel over whether nothing can be completed. Lem's language 'suicidally disowns itself'; Cloninger's apophasis allows no last word; Dworkin: 'there are no real absences, only replacements.'

fields.Thread: Three books whose authors say they wrote none of it: Kraus's Preface ('the most lurid fantasies are quotations'), Bäcker's notes ('Every part of transcript is a quotation'), Dillard's Author's Note ('I did not write a word of it'). Each concedes the same exceptions, order and cut: Bäcker's 'except in sequence, repetition, omission'; Dillard's 'Sometimes I dropped extra words; I never added a word'. Authorship moves into that parenthesis. They part on what the cut does to the source's intention: Kraus keeps it and turns it on the speaker (with the Grumbler as commentator); Bäcker keeps it and lets the isolated document convict itself, with no commentator; Dillard discards it ('the original authors' intentions were usually first to go') and adds delight. Bäcker's own note 16 sets Himmler's 'being emigrated' beside a participle quoted by Kraus, which is most likely the Grumbler's 'compulsorily enlisted' (II, 10: 'Universal conscription has turned mankind into a passive noun'). Dillard is the control case: same method, opposite effect.

fields.Thread: What should be done with the ashes of the dead? Browne believes 'our estranged and divided ashes shall unite againe' at 'the voyce of God', calls human preservations a 'fallacy in duration', and notes that 'Pharaoh is sold for balsoms'. Fedorov (via Groys's Russian Cosmism) turns Browne's palingenesis ('What the Art of man can doe...') into the sons' common task, with the museum as the instrument of resurrection. Malevich (via Zhilyaev's Avant-Garde Museology) answers: burn it, 'thousands of graveyards could be accommodated on one chemist's shelf', 'set up one pharmacy'. Browne's apothecary jar of Pharaoh and Malevich's pharmacy of Rubens are the same object valued oppositely. fields.Thread: Leroi-Gourhan argues the first graphism was a rhythmic series of incised lines, abstract from the start, later bent by writing into a 'needle-sharp, but also needle-thin' line subordinated to speech. Hudson's study of Agnes Martin's Night Sea (1963) supplies the case: a six-foot grid of scored, gilded lines ruled with threads borrowed from Lenore Tawney's loom, whose 'visual tremolo' records the arm; after it, Martin linearized her own practice.

fields.Thread: What a movement does the morning after the End fails to arrive. Scholem's Sabbatai Ṣevi follows three disconfirmations (imprisonment, apostasy, death), each producing a new doctrine: the 'Tower of Strength', the holy ruse/descent into the qelippah, occultation and the cave 'full of light'. Schweitzer's Quest makes the delay of the Parousia the origin of Christianity ('the non-occurrence of the Parousia', ch. XIX) and reports Reimarus's thesis that the disciples 'stole the body of Jesus and hid it'. Nikolaidis's The Coming, set in Ulcinj where Sabbatai died, has his followers burn a library so he can come again, and states the thesis outright: 'The non-occurrence of the catastrophe was a catastrophe' (ch. 9); epigraph from Kafka, the Messiah 'will come only on the day after his arrival'. Hinges: Renan (quoted by Scholem p. 689; a chapter in Schweitzer) and Scholem's own 'Readers of Paul's letters can learn a great deal from these later Jewish writings' (p. 803). Conflict: delay de-eschatologizes (Schweitzer), disconfirmation radicalizes into the paradox of 'a saint who sins' (Scholem), non-arrival is itself the catastrophe (Nikolaidis). The novel's Sabbatai, checked against Scholem: 9 August for the Ninth of Ab, 30 September for 17 September 1676.

fields.Thread: Three books about the interval in which someone lies still and waits for something they cannot make arrive. Kingsley reconstructs incubation as practice (Phōlarchos, 'lords of the lair', lying in caves in hesychia until a vision came) and reads Parmenides' poem as its record. Wallas (1926) takes the same word for the second of his four stages of thought (Preparation, Incubation, Illumination, Verification) and makes it mental hygiene. Benjamin (1927–34) lies on a hotel bed in Marseilles or a sofa in Berlin while a physician keeps the protocol, and seeks a 'profane illumination'. Wallas borrowed two stage-names from religious vocabulary; Kingsley restores the sacred sense of the first; Benjamin keeps the second without the sacred. Less obvious: all three hit the moment the subject cannot observe — Wallas's corona visible only in eclipse; Fränkel forbidden to take notes at the deepest point; Kingsley's priests 'in charge of the place'. Each needs a second party or stage (Verification, protocol-keeper, priest) to bring back what the first could not hold.

fields.Thread: Three books about a promise that outlives the person who made it. Kadare's Kostandin gave his mother his besa to bring Doruntine home. He dies, his mother curses him at the grave, and the dead man rides back. Agamben argues the curse is not added to the oath but co-originary with it, two outcomes of one act in which the speaker stakes himself on his word. Frayling's anthology carries the ballad's literary descendants (Bürger's 'Lenore' → 'the dead travel fast' in Dracula) and shows that the English vampire tale opens with a dying man extracting an oath (Byron's 'Fragment', 1816; Polidori, 1819). The oath runs in opposite directions: in Kadare it brings the dead back to deliver someone; in Polidori, 'Remember your oath' silences the living while the dead returns to take someone. In both, the curse half does the work: the mother's malediction, and the self-curse in Tolstoy's 'Vourdalak' ballad ('If I should break my oath, come to me after your death'). Agamben: 'It is from the oath—or, better, from perjury—that magic and spells are born.'

fields.Thread: Three books that take the relation, not the thing, as what carries meaning, and test the claim by removing a piece. Perec's Preamble: 'the parts do not determine the pattern, but the pattern determines the parts'. Life A User's Manual walks a building's cross-section one room per chapter (99 chapters for 100 squares; knight's tour unstated in the text) and ends with Bartlebooth dead, holding a W-shaped piece over an X-shaped hole. Moretti turns Hamlet into a network (characters = vertices, speech acts = edges) and deletes vertices: removing Hamlet then Horatio — flat, unmotivated, less central than Claudius — severs the Ghost and Fortinbras from the play. Hage & Harary supply the formal vocabulary (cutpoint, bridge, hamiltonian, eulerian) and find it already in anthropology: New Hebrides sand drawings, one continuous line, finger never lifted, nothing traced twice, are eulerian. Conflict over mathematics: Moretti 'unfortunately lack[s]' it and works by hand; H&H: 'the mathematics really must be made explicit'; Perec makes it explicit and hides it.

fields.Thread: Day 5 (uncredited use, suspected). Two suspicions, several nulls; no finding of plagiarism. (1) Girard, Job: The Victim of His People (8264, 1985/tr. Freccero 1987) uses 'a double crowd phenomenon' (ch. 15, p. 93) — the title of two chapters of Crowds and Power — without naming Canetti; yet Violence and the Sacred (7959, p. 131 n. 3) calls Crowds and Power 'the best treatment of the crowd's role in abolishing differences'. Girard changes the concept: Canetti's double crowd is two crowds facing each other (space); Girard's is one crowd that venerates and then persecutes one individual (time: 'Veneration is transformed into execration', p. 85). 'Double' is endemic in Girard, so independent arrival is possible; French original not checked. (2) Abbott, Vampires & a Reasonable Dictionary (6002): 'How does a country move from “crowds and power” to a self-conscious and skeptical democracy?' (Belgrade, 24 May 1998) — the title in quotation marks, unnamed: allusion. Nulls: onlyness (de Gennaro, Heidegger), 'moment of survival' (Bernhard, Negarestani), title echoes only in bibliographies (Thrift, Killing the Messiah); 15 coinages absent from 107 thematic titles not naming Canetti.
